title: Bhakti yoga: the nine forms of devotion; the Alvars and Nayanars; Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas; kirtan as method (4 of 7)
hook: a hunter who didn't know the rules offers Shiva everything, including his own eye
tomorrow: Bhakti yoga: the nine forms of devotion; the Alvars and Nayanars; Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas; kirtan as method (5 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Alvars, Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu. Andal's garland, and a singer carried in on a priest's shoulders. Today, their neighbors, the saints of Shiva.

A temple priest in the hills of the south arrives each morning to do the worship properly: the water, the flowers, the mantras, all in order. And every morning he finds the shrine a mess. Meat on the floor. Water splashed everywhere. Wilted wildflowers. Someone is getting in overnight and defiling it. He's heartbroken. So one night he hides, to catch whoever's doing it. What he sees, the story says, turns his idea of proper worship upside down.
screen: `A PRIEST AND HIS PERFECT RITUAL.` → `EVERY MORNING, A MESS.` → `ONE NIGHT HE HIDES.`

segments.voice: The Nayanars are the Alvars' neighbors: sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva. The poet Sekkizhar gathered their stories in the Periya Puranam, the great story. Three of them, Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, left hymns, the Tevaram, still sung in Shiva temples. And one of them is the hunter the priest saw that night. His name was Thinnan. He'd found the Shiva linga in the forest and fallen completely in love. He knew none of the rules, so he worshiped the way a hunter would. He carried water in his own mouth and poured it over the linga. He brought flowers tucked in his hair. He offered the best meat from his hunt, tasted first to make sure it was good. The priest watched, horrified. Then, the story says, one of the eyes on the linga began to bleed. Thinnan didn't hesitate. He cut out his own eye and pressed it into place. The bleeding stopped. Then the other eye began to bleed. He had one eye left, and he'd need to find the spot once he was blind, so he put his foot on the linga to mark it and raised the arrow. And Shiva stopped his hand. From that day he's been called Kannappa, the one who gave his eye. The Nayanars also include a woman poet, Karaikkal Ammaiyar, whom Shiva, the story says, called mother, and a laborer, Nandanar, kept outside the temple, who longed only to see Shiva dance. Love first. Rules, maybe, later.
screen: `SIXTY-THREE SAINTS OF SHIVA.` · `A HUNTER WHO KNEW NO RULES.` · `THE EYE THAT BLED.` · `KANNAPPA, WHO GAVE HIS EYE.` · then, large: `LOVE AS THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Think of the way you show love when nobody's grading you: clumsy, maybe too much, cooking, fixing things, showing up with the wrong flowers. See it without embarrassment, and let it be enough. If you pray, offer your own clumsy way of loving, the hunter's way, just as it is; if not, rest in it.
Bhakti yoga, through the Nayanars: sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva. Kannappa the hunter, who gave his eye, shows love that comes before the rules.
Your line: love as the road. Shiva took the hunter's clumsy love just as it came. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Tamil Shaiva temples, hymns of the Nayanars (the Tevaram and others) are sung in temple worship, images of the sixty-three saints often line the temple halls, and the Periya Puranam's stories, like Kannappa's, are retold at festivals and to children.

original.note: Tamil: nayanmar, the Nayanars, 'leaders' or 'masters'; the sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva.

what a scholar hears: Kannappa's story is set at Kalahasti (in today's Andhra Pradesh); the Tevaram of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar was compiled into the Tirumurai, the Tamil Shaiva canon, which closes with Sekkizhar's Periya Puranam.

chat.says: The hunter broke every rule of worship. Why is he remembered as a saint?
options: Because his love came first, and Shiva took it just as it came.
Because he secretly knew the rituals and did them all perfectly.
Because the priest taught him the proper way the next morning.
chat.meaning: Kannappa knew none of the rules, yet Shiva accepted his clumsy love and stopped his hand. Love first, rules maybe later.

Nayanars.meaning: sixty-three Tamil saints devoted to Shiva

Kannappa.meaning: the hunter-saint who gave his eye to Shiva

linga.meaning: the sacred form in which Shiva is worshiped

Periya Puranam.meaning: Sekkizhar's great book of the Nayanars' lives

Tevaram.meaning: hymns of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, sung in Shiva temples
